# Draft:Logistics of the 1992 Republican National Convention

Site selection
The two finalist cities that Houston had defeated to land the convention were New Orleans and San Diego. While Houston was the adopted hometown of the incumbent Republican president George H. W. Bush, when the location was announced, the party insisted that Bush had not used his influence to land the city the convention, and had only instructed the party to choose "the best site" for the convention. However, it was reported that Bush had indeed lobbied in favor his personal preference that his adopted mom,e city of Houston be selected.

Houston's bid
____
The Astrodome had been newly-renovated before its selection as the convention's location.
New Orleans' bid
New Orleans had been the location of the previous Republican National Convention in 1988.
San Diego's bid
San Diego had never before hosted a convention. It had originally been selected to host the 1972 Republican National Convention, but the convention's location was moved amid a scandal.

Convention executives
David J. Nash, who had experience in Hollywood production, served as the executive producer of the convention. Kyle Simmons served as the convention's spokesman.
Convention officers
Funding
The Houston Host Committee raised $4.3 million, primarily from corporate donors. Party officials hailed this as the most ever raised for a convention.
In 1992, both major party nominating conventions each received $11 million from the federal government to assist in aspects of convention logistics.
Volunteers
The host committee recruited thousands of local volunteers to aid in operations. This proved challenging, with local residents largely unenthusiastic towards volunteering, and the host committee ultimately falling 1,000 shy of its initial target to recruit 12,000 volunteers. Volunteers were used to fill an assortment roles, including serving as ushers, babysitters, and drivers.
Separately from the host committee, the organization Clean Houston had set a target to recruit 15,000 volunteers to help remove litter from Houston roads ahead of the convention, but only managed to recruit 7,000 volunteers. This was roughly half the number ofvolunteers that the organization was able to recruit for the same task ahead of the 16th G7 summit in 1990. However, even with a much smaller number of volunteers, Clean Houston was able to remove a greater amount of litter ahead of the convention than it had head of the G7 summit.
Conversion the Astrodome for use as a convention hall
Efforts to convert the Astrodome ahead of the convention required 500,000 man-hours.
Necessitated Astros road trip
To accommodate the convention and its set-up, the Houston Astros, the Major League Baseball team which played at the Astrodome, played 26 consecutive away games over 28 days, the longest Major League Baseball "road trip" since the Philadelphia Phillies played 27 away games in 28 days in 1944. This made the Astro's road trip was the longest taken by any Major League Baseball team since the adoption of air travel. Additionally, the National Football League's Houston Oilers were forced to play all their preseason games on the road.
The Major League Baseball Players Association had filed an unsuccessful grievance in October 1991 in an attempt to block the planned 26-game road trip by the Astros. The Major League Baseball Players Association took issue with the Houston Sports Association (owners of the Astrodome) renting the stadium to the Republican National Convention organizers from July 27 through August 23, 1992, without first seeking permission from the National League, and their grievance sought to shorten the length of the road trip, arguing that the 26-game road trip went against the National League's constitution.
Conversion of interior space
speaking at the convention]]
For the convention, the stadium was arranged to seat 36,000 people. Production designer Robert Keene, an Emmy Award-winner, was involved in the venue setup.
The Astrodome was a much larger space than Madison Square Garden, where the Democrats had held their convention in July. The massive interior space of the stadium created challenges for its conversion into a suitable venue for a convention. Organizers held concern that the size of the venue would make the convention's podium appear miniscule. To negate this concern, the podium and its backdrop were constructed at a grand scale. The podium (stage) had a depth of , and its backdrop featured a faux-limestone square-topped proscenium arch standing  high, bookended on each side by panels featuring 49 television screens. The front of the podium was situated roughly where a baseball field's second base typically stood in the venue. In order to hasten installation, the podium structure was prefabricated. It was first assembled at a warehouse, then disassembled and transported for reassembly in the Astrodome. President Bush made a request that the stage be designed to create less of a barrier between the president and the attendees, which designers obliged by making it  lower to the convention floor than the 1988 convention stage, and making its stage-end railing translucent. With this change made, the stage stood  above the convention floor. ________
The balloon drop at the end of the convention was touted to be four-times the scale of the 1992 Democratic convention's balloon drop, involving 250,000 balloons (which organizers claimed was a world record. The pieces of confetti Republicans utilized were biodegradable.
To further address the cavernous scale of the venue, a massive curtain weighing , was installed to block-off the portions of its space not being used.
Sound dampening material was placed throughout the venue to decrease the echo of the venue, out of concerns that venue's existing acoustics would make it hard for speakers' speeches to be clearly heard.
Shortly before the start of work to convert the convention, local officials ordered for an independent inspection to be conducted to ensure that the venue's roof could safely support the weight of the curtain, lights, and speakers that were to be temporarily-suspended from it during the convention. Inspectors cleared the project to proceed.
Electrical and telephone systems were installed in and around the stadium to meet the demands of the convention, and were reinforced with aim for them to safely withstand the potential weather effects of a hurricane.
An indoor fireworks display was set up inside of the stadium for the convention, being launched alongside the balloon drop at the conclusion of Bush's acceptance speech.
Adjacent facilities and exterior grounds
The Astrohall, a convention center complex adjacent to the stadium, was used as a workspace for news media. Hiding a request by President Bush, organizers converted the adjacent Astroarena into a space dubbed the "American Spirit Pavilion", which featured exhibits displaying curiosities such as a section of the Berlin Wall and a bronze statue of Bush standing  tall.
A giant topiary of an elephant (a symbol of the Republican Party) was created outside of the Astrodome. One of the other more elaborate decorative fixtures was a large chocolate sculpture of an elephant weighing  and standing  tall. Organizers also brought in a live elephant, with its feet painted red, white, and blue (the colors on the flag of the United States).
Convention production and scheduling
Republicans sought to deliver the Bush-Dan Quayle ticket a division-free convention that highlighted talking points in favor of Bush's re-election. Party officials were cautious about shaping the schedule of speakers. As the convention approached, this became a more challenging task, as the 1992 Republican primaries surfaced some ideological divides in the party. Additionally, Vice President Quayle's proclivity for misspeaking had increasingly become perceived as a liability to Bush's re-election chances.
Each night of the convention was given a theme. The first night was "The American Spirit and the World", highlighting foreign policy. The second night was "The American Spirit and the Nation", highlighting domestic policy. The third night was "The American Spirit and the Family", focused on characterizing Republicans as "pro-family" and Democrats as "anti-family". The final night was "The American Spirit and the Presidency", focusing on Bush's deservingness of a second term.
Executive producer David J. Nash caught to limit all but the most marquee speakers to limit their remarks to a maximum length of ten minutes.

Hotels
President Bush stayed at the Houstonian Hotel and Conference Center. A giant topiary of an elephant was created outside of the hotel, which was one of two such topiaries created for the convention (the other being at the Astrodome).
Delegate hotels
*Hilton Nassau Bay: Colorado
*Holiday Inn Intercontinental: Wisconsin
*Holiday Inn-NASA: South Dakota
*Intercontinental Airport Marriott: Pennsylvania
*Marriott Galleria: Indiana
*Marriott West Loop Hotel: North Carolina, West Virginia
*Sheraton Grand: New Hampshire
*South Shore Harbour Resort: Alabama
Related events
Convention-related events, including official receptions and parties, were held at a variety of venues across the Houston region.
The Astroarena was also the site of a "Red, White, and Boots" party hosted by U.S. Senator Phil Gramm on the opening day of the convention. Other venues that held official secondary events included Cody's Rooftop Jazzbar & Grill in Houston's Montrose neighborhood; the Great Southwest Equestrian Center in Katy; Cadillac Bar & Grill, Clear Lake Yacht Club, Vargo's restaurant, and Black-Eyed Pea restaurant.
Other events were held at various private residences, including residences in The Woodlands, and the Memorial neighborhood of Houston,
Groups and companies that hosted events included the Log Cabin Republicans and Enron.
Transit
With the host location being one of America's most vast, sprawling, and decentralized metro areas, most delegates needed to take long highway commutes between their hotels to the Astrodome. The Astrodome itself was located  away from the city's main downtown. Significant highway travel was also required to attend parties and other secondary events were held at sites spread across the various reaches of the metro region. Some such events were held as far away as the Galveston Bay area,  southeast of the city of Houston.
Attendees could not be expected to arrive at the Astrodome by any means other than motor vehicle, as the venue stood at the center of a  complex with vast surrounding parking lots, and the summer heat in Texas would make the trek across those parking lots unbearable. Since traffic in-and-out of the complex had proven itself notoriously slow for large events where spectators arrived in personal automobiles (such as Houston Oiler football games), a vast fleet of buses was used to transport delegates.
To facilitate the challenge of ferrying delegates long distances across a vast region, a transportation control center was established.
Various different groups involved in the convention operated bus routes for attendees in a similar fashion to mass-transit systems. Additionally, the Houston Galleria mall (a major shopping destination in Houston) ran its own route of shuttle buses to the mall during the convention, which were decorated with large elephant emblems.
In addition to moving people, the convention also necessitated complex transit logistics regarding supplies. For instance, the distribution of the 6,000 welcoming gift bags delegates were to be greeted with at their hotels required a fleet of trucks loaned by local companies. This same fleet was also used to distribute additional souvenir gifts each day to delegates' hotels.
